note: Stage 1 shard 2: ten high-frequency evaluative families. Charge is judgement on the family's axis; register lives in usage labels.

members.tone: Grudging - good, but only moderately, and the word admits it.
Clears the bar and no more; in speech it often signals mild disappointment.
Meets the requirement - the language of reports and inspections, not of praise.
Warm but modest - better than expected without being remarkable.
The plain word of approval - broad, safe, and unemphatic.
examples: a good meal and good company

members.tone: Praises dependability rather than brilliance - built to last.
Everyday enthusiasm - the common word for real approval.
examples: That was a great film.

members.tone: Unqualified praise - at the top of its class.
Surpassing praise, with a note of polish and craft.
examples: a superb performance from the whole cast

members.tone: Old-fashioned cheer - now often used ironically.
Period slang; using it today reads as deliberately retro.
Hearty and old-fashioned approval.
Damns by middling - not bad enough to condemn, not good enough to praise.
members.explanation: The insult is the absence of merit, not the presence of fault.
examples: a mediocre film that nobody remembers

members.tone: The plain word of disapproval - broad and unemphatic.
examples: bad weather
a bad decision

members.tone: Casual disgust - everyday, forceful, and slightly coarse.
Thoroughly bad, with a hint of moral distaste.
Crude dismissal - fine among friends, out of place in writing.
Strong condemnation, common enough to have lost some of its force.
examples: an awful mistake

members.tone: Emphatic disapproval with a formal, slightly literary edge.
Blunt and total - among the strongest everyday condemnations.
Severe and formal - originally of cruelty, now also of quality.
members.explanation: Carries a residue of moral horror even when used of a meal.
examples: atrocious handwriting
atrocious treatment of prisoners

members.tone: Moral revulsion - condemns rather than criticises.
Formal censure, expecting the reader to share the judgement.
Affectionate scolding, mostly of children - too light for real fault.
The softened word - avoids naming a deficit outright.
Mild and often jokey - failing to grasp what is plain.
Gently disparaging, common in British use.
Formal reproach - slow to understand, and perhaps unwilling to.
The blunt, wounding word - a flat verdict on someone's mind.
members.explanation: Direct enough that most speakers reach for a softer term when they mean it kindly.
examples: It was a stupid thing to say.

members.tone: Harsh and casual; also an older, now offensive word for mute.
members.explanation: Avoid of people - it insults rather than describes.

members.tone: Faults the judgement rather than the intelligence - a wise person can act foolishly.
examples: a foolish risk to take with someone else's money

members.tone: Withering - stupidity so complete it deserves contempt.
Silliness with self-satisfaction attached.
Empty of sense - condemns the content, not the person.
Crude and mocking.
British informal - vacant and hopeless with it.
Warm and everyday - quick to learn, most often said of the young.
examples: a bright student who asks good questions

members.tone: Common approval of quickness; in some uses it edges toward cunning.
Praises ingenuity - though 'too clever' turns it into a fault.
members.explanation: Approving of resourcefulness, with a faint warning attached.
examples: a clever solution nobody else saw

members.tone: Quick to learn - formal and slightly old-fashioned.
The neutral, respectable word - approving without flourish.
examples: an intelligent reading of a difficult text

members.tone: Praises speed of understanding rather than depth.
Affectionate and slightly teasing admiration.
Exceptional intelligence - the strongest ordinary compliment.
members.explanation: Marks someone out from the merely clever.
examples: a brilliant mathematician

members.tone: Cleverness that sparkles in company.
Sharp and penetrating - praise for incisive thought.
Pleasing but slight - delicate rather than striking, and faintly diminishing when used of adults.
members.explanation: Approving, though it implies charm rather than power.
examples: a pretty little garden

members.tone: Old-fashioned approval of pleasant looks.
Scottish and northern English warmth - healthy and pleasing.
Praises strong, well-proportioned looks; used of men, and of women to suggest dignity over prettiness.
Plain, unfussy approval - the everyday compliment.
Warm and affectionate - beauty that moves the feelings, not just the eye.
The full word - unreserved and applicable to anything from a face to an argument.
examples: a beautiful morning
a beautiful proof

members.tone: Beauty of fine detail - praise for delicacy and craft.
Dazzling and enthusiastic - beauty that stops you.
Striking enough to arrest attention.
Overwhelming beauty - lush and a little theatrical.
British slang for sexually attractive - casual and now somewhat dated.
Understated - withholds beauty rather than asserting ugliness.
members.explanation: The gentlest way to say it.

members.tone: Polite avoidance - unremarkable rather than unattractive.
Offends the eye - used more comfortably of things than of people.
The blunt word, and a wounding one of a person.
members.explanation: Passes flat judgement on appearance; most speakers soften it when they can.
examples: an ugly concrete tower
There is no kind way to call someone ugly.

members.tone: Distorted to the point of unsettling - beyond plain ugliness.
Ugliness that frightens; also used of moral wrong.
Extreme and repellent - among the harshest words available.
examples: a hideous scar left by the fire

members.tone: Ugliness that actively drives people away.
Crude insult built from an obscenity - offensive in any setting.
Temporary and undramatic - short of money this month, not poor in life.
Casual and often self-applied - out of money right now.
examples: I'm broke until payday.

members.tone: British slang, cheerfully blunt.
The plain word for a lasting condition - factual, but heavy enough that officials avoid it.
examples: a poor family in a rich country

members.tone: Genteel and bookish - poverty at a polite distance.
Absolute and vivid - not a coin left.
Frames poverty as requiring help; of a person's temperament it means something else entirely.
Made poor - the word implies something was taken away.
members.explanation: Points at a cause rather than blaming the poor.

members.tone: The legal and administrative term for qualifying poverty.
Total and grave - without even the means to live.
examples: The fire left them destitute.

members.tone: Poverty as an affliction that has struck, not a state chosen.
The modest way to say it - enough money, and no wish to discuss it.
Plainly better off than most, without ostentation.
Wealth read as the reward of success - approving.
The neutral term of economists and estate agents.
Substantial and settled money - more dignified than 'rich'.
The plain word - direct, and sometimes faintly accusing depending on who says it.
examples: rich enough never to check a price

members.tone: Wealth as a class marker, often said with a raised eyebrow.
Temporarily well supplied - this week, not for life.
Blunt and slightly envious - conspicuously rich.
examples: Her family is absolutely loaded.

members.tone: Comfortably moneyed, with a wry edge.
Willing to try - courage as good sportsmanship rather than heroism.
Courage as endurance - staying in when it hurts.
Affectionate praise for spirit, often of someone small taking on something large.
The plain, universal praise - facing what frightens you.
examples: a brave decision to speak up

members.tone: Weightier than 'brave' - implies moral choice, not just nerve.
Chivalrous courage - noble and old-fashioned.
Heroic register, at home in battle and legend.
Steadfast courage - praise with a Victorian ring.
Courage defined by what failed to stop it.
The superlative - courage as legend.
Courage beyond what could be asked of anyone.
Gentle - shyness rather than failure of nerve, and rarely an accusation.
Lacking boldness - mild, and often used of a task rather than a person.
Names the fear without judging the person for it.
The plain accusation - fear that led to failing others.
members.explanation: Condemns the choice, not the feeling.
examples: a cowardly refusal to take responsibility

members.tone: Playground taunt - mocking rather than grave.
Old-fashioned scorn from a theory that pale organs meant no courage.
Blunt slang accusation of cowardice.
Abject cowardice - formal and thoroughly contemptuous.
Cowardice joined to malice; now often played for comedy.
Bookish contempt - small-spirited in the face of difficulty.
Abject cowardice - formal and thoroughly contemptuous.
